text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

footnotes.text: The Greek 'logos' is rendered "Word," the traditional English choice, kept here for its familiarity and its rhythm in reading aloud. No single English term captures the full range of 'logos': it can mean spoken word, message, account, reason, or the ordering principle behind reality. Alternatives such as "Message," "Reason," or leaving the term untranslated as "Logos" each capture one facet while losing others. The preposition 'pros' with the accusative is translated "with," though it carries a dynamic sense of facing or being turned toward someone, suggesting relationship rather than mere proximity. In the third clause the Greek word order places 'theos' first for emphasis; because English cannot reproduce this without awkwardness, the clause is rendered in normal order, "and the Word was God." The threefold repetition of "and the Word" mirrors the deliberate cadence of the Greek and is well suited to being read aloud.

'En archē' echoes the opening words of Genesis in Greek, inviting the reader to hear this as a new creation account. The verb 'ēn' is imperfect — continuous existence, not a coming into being — and stands in sharp contrast to the aorist 'egeneto' ("came to be") used of created things in verse 3 and of John the Baptist in verse 6. In the final clause 'theos' lacks the article while 'ho logos' has it: this grammar marks 'ho logos' as the subject and 'theos' as the predicate, describing what the Word is rather than identifying him as the same person as the Father. Greek regularly omits the article on a predicate noun placed before the verb, so the absence of the article here does not by itself make the term indefinite.

Three claims are made in quick succession: the Word existed before creation, the Word was distinct enough from God to be "with" him, and the Word shared fully in what God is. The early church appealed to this verse in formulating the doctrine of the Trinity and of Christ's full divinity. Readings that render the last clause "a god" or "divine" have been proposed but sit uneasily with the Gospel's later confession of Jesus as "my Lord and my God." Others have read "the Word was God" as identifying the Word with the Father, but the preceding clause distinguishes them.

'Logos' carried weight in more than one world of thought. In Greek philosophy, particularly among the Stoics, it named the rational principle ordering the cosmos. In Jewish tradition, the word of the Lord created and spoke through the prophets, and Wisdom was portrayed as present with God at creation; Aramaic synagogue paraphrases spoke of God's 'Memra' (Word) as his acting presence. A first-century reader from either background would have recognized the term, and then been startled by the claim in verse 14 that this Word became flesh.

The opening of this Gospel has long held a prominent place in Christian worship, read at the great festival of the Nativity and, in some traditions, recited at the close of the liturgy as a summary of the faith.

text: He was in the beginning with God.
All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being.

versions.text: All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.
versions.explanation: The relative clause 'ὃ γέγονεν' ('that which has come into being') is left untranslated. Whether it is joined to the end of verse 3 or to the beginning of verse 4, it should appear somewhere in the text; at present the words are simply dropped. A footnote could note the ancient variation in punctuation, which allows the alternative reading 'What has come into being in him was life.'

text: In him was life, and that life was the light of all people.

versions.text: In him was life, and that life was the light of humanity.
versions.explanation: 'τῶν ἀνθρώπων' is a plural referring to human beings; 'the light of humanity' reads as an abstraction and is slightly awkward when read aloud. 'The light of all people' keeps the plural sense and flows better in oral reading.

text: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.
There came a man sent from God, whose name was John.
He came as a witness, to testify about the light, so that through him all might believe.
He himself was not the light, but came to testify about the light.

versions.text: He was not the light; he came to testify about the light.
versions.explanation: The emphatic pronoun 'ἐκεῖνος' and the strong adversative 'ἀλλά' are both flattened by the semicolon. Rendering the contrast explicitly ('He himself... but') reflects the Greek emphasis and gives a cleaner spoken cadence.

text: The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.
He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, yet the world did not know him.
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not receive him.
But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God—
children born not of blood, nor of the desire of the flesh, nor of a husband's will, but of God.
And the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory of the Father's only Son, full of grace and truth.
John testified about him, crying out: "This is the one I spoke of: the one who comes after me has surpassed me, because he was before me."
For out of his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.
For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
No one has ever seen God. The only Son, himself God, who is at the Father's side, has made him known.
This is the testimony John gave when the Jews of Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask him, "Who are you?"
He confessed and did not deny it; he confessed, "I am not the Messiah."
So they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" He answered, "No."
Then they said to him, "Who are you? We need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"
He said, "I am a voice crying out in the wilderness: 'Make straight the way of the Lord'—as the prophet Isaiah said."
Now those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.
They questioned him: "Why then are you baptizing, if you are not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?"
John answered them, "I baptize with water. Among you stands one you do not know,
the one who comes after me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie."
This took place at Bethany on the other side of the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and said, "Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
This is the one I spoke about when I said, 'After me comes a man who has surpassed me, because he was before me.'
I myself did not know him, but I came baptizing with water so that he might be revealed to Israel."
And John testified: "I saw the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and remain on him.
I myself did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize with water told me, 'The man on whom you see the Spirit come down and remain—he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'
And I have seen it, and I have testified that this is the Chosen One of God.

versions.text: And I have seen it, and I testify that this is the Chosen One of God."
versions.explanation: Both verbs are perfect ('ἑώρακα... μεμαρτύρηκα'); the shift to the present 'I testify' breaks the parallel between the two clauses that the Greek deliberately sets up.

text: The next day John was standing there again with two of his disciples,
and as he watched Jesus walking by, he said, "Look, the Lamb of God!"
When the two disciples heard him say this, they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned, saw them following, and asked, "What are you looking for?" They said, "Rabbi"—which means Teacher—"where are you staying?"
"Come and see," he said. So they went and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour—four in the afternoon.

versions.text: "Come and see," he said. So they went and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.
versions.explanation: Modern hearers will not know what "the tenth hour" means. A brief in-text gloss or footnote clarifying it was about four in the afternoon aids oral comprehension.

text: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, was one of the two who heard what John said and followed Jesus.

versions.text: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, was one of the two who had heard John and followed Jesus.
versions.explanation: The Greek ἀκουσάντων παρὰ Ἰωάννου means "heard from John" (i.e., heard John's testimony), not simply "heard John." Supplying "what John said" clarifies the sense while keeping the clarifying substitution of "Jesus" for the ambiguous pronoun.

text: He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah"—that is, the Christ.

versions.text: The first thing he did was to find his brother Simon and tell him, "We have found the Messiah"—that is, the Christ.
versions.explanation: The Greek πρῶτον most naturally means Andrew found his brother first (before other actions or before the other disciple did), not that this was the very first thing he did. The rendering also flattens τὸν ἀδελφὸν τὸν ἴδιον ("his own brother") and is wordier than needed for oral reading.

text: And he brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon son of John. You will be called Cephas"—which means Peter.
The next day Jesus decided to leave for Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me."
Philip was from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael and told him, "We have found the one Moses wrote about in the law, and the prophets as well: Jesus son of Joseph, from Nazareth."
"Nazareth! Can anything good come from there?" Nathanael asked. "Come and see," said Philip.
When Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him, he said of him, "Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit."
"How do you know me?" Nathanael asked. Jesus answered, "I saw you while you were still under the fig tree, before Philip called you."
Nathanael replied, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel."
Jesus answered him, "You believe because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see far greater things than that."

versions.text: Jesus said, "You believe because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see far greater things than that."
versions.explanation: The Greek has the full formula "answered and said to him"; "answered him" better reflects that this is a response to Nathanael's confession and restores the omitted αὐτῷ.

text: And he added, "Truly, truly I tell you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
